1:
Henry counts the credentials one by one, and the tally is the point. They were the house of Jacob, with a place and a name in the visible church; they were called by the name of Israel, which signifies a prince with God; they had come forth out of the waters of Judah and so were of the royal tribe, which held when the rest revolted; they swore by the name of the Lord and took an oath of allegiance; they called themselves of the holy city; and they stayed themselves upon the God of Israel. Then the whole soars and sinks in a phrase, since none of it was in truth or righteousness. Clarke, surveying the chapter, states its purpose as leaving them no pretext for ascribing any portion of their success to their idols.

The address is narrower than its opening words suggest. Ellicott takes the clause about the waters of Judah to limit the wider terms Jacob and Israel to the southern exiles, and finds the ideal attributes pressed deliberately against their actual state. Wesley reads the figure as descent, the lineage flowing from its progenitor as water from a fountain, and takes the swearing as one act of religion standing for the whole profession. Gill allows them a name and a place in the house of the God of Jacob, but only in profession. Keil and Delitzsch mark the structure rather than the sense: the summons and the description of those summoned come first, and only then does the address of Jehovah begin.

That the honours are being recited ironically is the common judgment. Ellicott says the words of praise carry a touch of irony, since those who boasted so were not true citizens of Zion and had not entered into what their confession implied. Calvin puts it more sharply: the prophet uses the honourable name not to speak respectfully but to shame a false boast, and the Israel he addresses is the spurious one that had nothing left but the name. He explains the vehemence by circumstance. The prophet was not sent to the Babylonians but foretold their fall so the captives might wait calmly; and foreseeing how hard they would be in captivity, caring no more for the promises than for empty fables, he was driven to speak severely.

The holy city draws the same treatment. Calvin grants that Jerusalem ought to have been holy, God having consecrated her to himself, and says she had prostituted herself to iniquities so great that she scarcely retained any holiness, while those who lived in her reckoned it enough to shelter under the shadow of the temple. Gill turns it forward at those who now call themselves fellow citizens with the saints and of the household of God while they are strangers to both. Henry says the same in a sentence, that many who are themselves unholy are proud of their relation to the church, and adds that captives in Babylon valued their interest in the city out of little more than jealousy for their native country.

Staying upon God is the last of the claims and the most searching. Calvin distinguishes it from the real thing: good men trust God with the whole heart, while hypocrites make pretensions to his name, are intoxicated by an unfounded belief, and boast that God will assist them and not cast off his people, as if he wished to encourage their wickedness. Wesley says the same in five words, not a true faith but a vain confidence. Calvin then finds the closing title a threat rather than a comfort, added so that men sheltering falsely under it might know he loses nothing of his authority by being misrepresented. Henry, hearing the same title, has them argue the opposite, that the Lord of hosts is their God and they are therefore happy and very great.
3:
Ellicott counts this the seventh time the prophet presses divine foreknowledge, and notices the target has shifted: earlier it was urged against the no-faith of the heathen, here against the little faith of Judah. Gill reaches back for the former things to what was told Abraham: the sojourn in Egypt, the affliction, the coming out with great substance, the land taken from its inhabitants. Calvin thinks the reference is not to the release from Babylon but to earlier benefits, and adds a point about the audience: the words were meant not only for those then living but for those who would live through the captivity, so that when the thing came they might recall it had been foretold and take consolation from that.

The reason given for the advance notice is the people's hardness, and it produces the boldest sentence in the chapter. Calvin says God acted more liberally towards them than he ought to have done, using an excellent remedy on a depravity otherwise incurable; he adds that this was not the only end in view, since the chief use of doctrine belongs to believers who submit gently. On the figure he is precise: sinews are hard but can be bent, and the point of calling the neck iron is that here there is no bending at all, while the brazen forehead denotes impudence. Keil and Delitzsch render the words an iron clasp and a brow of brass. Wesley draws the same inference, that clearer demonstrations were given because the nation was unbelieving. Ellicott observes that what is foreseen is not only the conquests of a deliverer but the obduracy of the delivered.

Why idols come into it at all is a question Calvin raises himself, since the Jews professed one God. His answer is that association with the nations had corrupted them and they had degenerated so far into superstition as to forget God entirely; he recalls Ezekiel carried in vision to a sanctuary polluted with idols. Ellicott says the same from the other end, that in Egypt as in Babylon they remained a stiff-necked people inclined to credit their deliverance to another god and worship it in a graven image. Calvin adds that the prediction was designed so none of the event could be assigned to fortune, since men rob God of his glory and would leave him a bare and empty name.

What the new things are divides them. Wesley identifies them with the deliverance out of Babylon by the promised conqueror. Ellicott puts them further off, treating that conquest as one of the former things and reserving the new for what lies in a more distant future. Clarke works on the imperative, reporting a manuscript and a version that read it differently, suspecting the word should be behold, and admitting he has rendered the clause somewhat paraphrastically. Calvin declines the usual reading and takes the word as a duty laid on the hearer: since the Lord has spoken, it is your business to examine and attend, and it is our own sluggishness that loses what comes from his mouth, so pleading ignorance is vain.

The word created draws careful handling. Gill reports an interpretation glossing it as decreed, and corrects it, since no new decrees are made and what was decreed of old is here only revealed. Wesley agrees it means brought to light as things are by creation. Ellicott finds the verb unusual for historical events: what had lain from the beginning in the mind of God is now first manifested, kept in store to make men wonder. He gives a reason for the reserve, that the people were unprepared and the truth would only have increased their condemnation. Calvin ends with the new name given once the mask is off, and takes the womb to mean not their origin as a nation but the deliverance out of Egypt.
9:
Why so guilty a people was not destroyed is answered twice over by Ellicott. After the manner of men, had God cut off his chosen the nations would have judged him capricious; and taking the name as the symbol of character, the sparing asserts his own everlasting righteousness and love, as one willing to save rather than destroy. Henry prefers to render the verb as stifling the anger rather than deferring it, and grounds the mercy in the same place, that the people bore God's name and their destruction would have set the enemy blaspheming. Gill says plainly it was for no merit of theirs. Wesley makes it all vindication, that God may be praised for his power, faithfulness and goodness.

Calvin finds two uses in the announcement, pointed at two different moments. During the captivity believers needed supporting so that they might not lose courage; and once permission to return arrived they needed humbling, so that they would ascribe the deliverance to nothing but undeserved goodness. He then turns the verse into an argument, that since remission here is made freely for God's name's sake, the schoolmen's distinction collapses, which refuses to allow that the remission of punishment is undeserved on the ground that satisfaction has been made to divine justice. Clarke's contribution is textual: a particle standing redundantly in the later verse, absent there from several versions, he judges to have migrated, and restores it here.

The refining that is not with silver is the chapter's difficulty, and Gill sets out the options rather than choosing. Silver is what gets refined, not a refining agent, so that cannot be the sense; it may mean not in a furnace of silver, or, with several versions and the Targum, in a furnace of poverty, the trial being by adversity and not prosperity; or not into silver, as though the labour were lost; or not for the sake of silver, God being no gainer by their afflictions. Clarke cuts through by changing a letter, reading like silver instead of with silver on the authority of the Latin, and adds that the word rendered furnace means properly the crucible in which the metal is melted.

On what the clause is for they converge remarkably. Clarke says that silver when purified leaves no dross at all, and had God done that here he would have consumed them altogether. Wesley says the same: silver stays in the fire until every trace of dross is gone, and such rigour would have consumed them. Henry adds that they would then be always in the furnace, since they are all dross. Calvin sharpens it: silver at least contains something pure, whereas in us nothing would be found but chaff, so in the trial God measures what we can bear and by his Spirit makes profitable what would otherwise be destruction. Ellicott, who thinks the figure may rest on some lost process of ancient metallurgy, reaches the same conclusion, that the discipline was less fierce than a refiner's.

The next verb splits them. Clarke and Ellicott both prefer tried to chosen, Clarke citing a manuscript and the eastern versions. Henry keeps the choosing and makes it the point, that affliction is no bar to God's choice but subservient to his purpose; Wesley keeps it too and reads a second choosing of a people God had in a manner rejected. On the last verse they agree again that the words about the name have dropped from the Hebrew and must be supplied. Calvin calls the question one of the kind Hebrew writers use for what is absurd, and draws consolation from it, that God has tied our salvation to his own glory. Wesley adds that a failure to rescue would have given idolaters colour for their claims, and Keil and Delitzsch mark the summons to hear that opens each half of the chapter.
12:
The address has changed since the chapter opened, and Calvin catches it in a figure. At the start the prophet showed that the Jews falsely assumed the name and gloried in it idly; here God calls Israel his called. It is as if a father rebuking his son should call him a bastard and then own him as his son: they are so degenerate that he might justly reject them, and though they deserve no such honour, he still pays regard to his own calling, which no ingratitude can set aside. Gill notes the same shift, that Jacob and Israel are described differently from the chapter's beginning, now that God has declared his designs of grace. Wesley reads it as a calling out of the world to be a peculiar people.

Ellicott places the section rather than glossing it. The prophet is nearing the end of the first great division of his book, and this is a condensed epitome of the preceding chapters, asserting the oneness, eternity, omnipotence and omniscience of God. Keil and Delitzsch describe the same movement as a continued exhortation, in which Israel learns the incomparable nature of God from a redemption prepared in word and deed, so that the whole future turns on the attitude it now takes to his commandments. Clarke supplies two textual repairs: several manuscripts and two old editions add my servant after Jacob, which he judges dropped from the present text, and the conjunction in the clause about the last is better read as a simple and.

On the making of the world Gill preserves a distinction from the Jewish commentators, that the hand which laid the earth's foundation is the left, the heavens being given to the right hand and the earth the less honourable work; he refers the founding to the Wisdom and Word and Son of God. Calvin refuses to labour the verb, saying it makes no difference whether God measured the heavens or upheld them. On the first he finds a wisdom that adjusted the vast expanse so exactly that it is neither nearer the earth nor further than order requires, with nothing jarring in it; on the second, a power holding the huge mass in continual motion without tottering or leaning. Wesley reads the standing up of the hosts as a readiness to execute commands.

Who is summoned to assemble is disputed. Ellicott takes the challenge to be addressed, as before, to the worshippers of idols. Gill and Calvin take it for the Jews, Calvin adding that the unbelieving have no ears and are not invited to hear, and that a people to whom God had revealed himself above all nations was the less excusable for undervaluing the treasure. He hears God offering them the floor, permitting any objection publicly, as men confident of their cause invite their adversaries to produce arguments. On the one whom the Lord has loved they agree it is the deliverer, though Ellicott thinks the pleasure and the arm that follow more probably God's.

Ellicott adds the finest observation here, that the word for the beloved alludes to the name of Israel's great king, so the foreign conqueror is to be a second David, beloved of the Lord. Clarke cites an old Greek version rendering the clause the same way and names the man plainly. Calvin finds a double emphasis in the repeated pronoun of the next verse: that none but the God of Israel has spoken of future and hidden things, and that since he never deceives, all he has foretold must come about. He gives the prophecy two objects, that the captives may expect deliverance and afterwards not imagine it came by human help or chance; and the conqueror prospers not by desert but because God chose to use him. Gill puts it that not one word of the Lord ever fails.
16:
The verse calls the hearers closer, and the distance is taken to be moral rather than spatial. Calvin says they stood far off not in space but in the agreement of the heart, and that drawing near means laying aside our natural dispositions and becoming ready to hear, which must proceed from grace, since we are never prepared unless God leads us; he hears in the invitation both a kindness going out to meet them and a reproach for the revolt that made it necessary. Henry makes the point practically: those who would understand what God says must approach him and come as near as they can, for those who draw nigh may depend on it that his secret will be with them.

Who is being called is less agreed. Clarke reports a manuscript adding the words O ye nations after the summons, and thinks it probably genuine, since this verse and the two before it are addressed to the idolatrous nations and reproach their gods. Ellicott reads the address as made to Israel. Gill takes it for the Jews and hears a call to attend the ministry of Christ; Calvin too takes it for the Jews, reproaching them with ingratitude. Clarke stands alone, and the difference matters: on his reading the verse is a challenge thrown at idolaters, on theirs an appeal to a covenant people who ought already to have listened.

What is denied is obscurity, heard against a particular background. Henry has God speaking publicly from the top of Sinai and in the chief places of concourse, not delivering his oracles obscurely or ambiguously but so that they might be understood. Ellicott's paraphrase makes the contrast explicit, that the prophet has not from the beginning spoken in dark ambiguous speeches like the oracles of the heathen. Clarke notes that one family of Greek copies adds a clause about not speaking in a dark place of the earth; he thinks it stood there very early, since two versions made from that Greek carry it, but suspects a copyist supplied it from the parallel passage, the sense not requiring it.

The next clause is compressed almost past construing. Clarke takes the word usually rendered there as a verb rather than an adverb, so that instead of there am I the sense becomes I had decreed it, and attaches a history to it: from the time the conqueror's expedition was planned, God was managing the whole by the economy of his providence. Calvin reads the presence as proved by the outcome, since what God uttered with his mouth was carried into execution by his own strength, so in accomplishing everything he gave tokens of having been there. Wesley takes it the same way, that from the time he first spoke he was there to effect what he foretold, and reads the not speaking in secret as covering either the prophetic ministry or the whole covenant.

Then the speaker changes, and four answers are given. Gill and Henry both hear the great prophet, Henry adding that the Spirit appears as a person distinct from the Father and the Son with divine authority to send prophets, so that whom God sends the Spirit sends. Wesley takes the sent one to be Isaiah, a type of Christ, letting the reference reach both. Ellicott finds the prophet appearing abruptly in his own person at the close, and thinks he may be the speaker throughout; he records two further constructions, one referring the words to the servant of the Lord, another making the Spirit the object of the verb rather than its subject, which is the order Clarke prefers. Calvin refuses both leading readings, calling the application to Christ a forced interpretation the prophet never meant, and the application to the prophet unsuitable, since such a discourse could not be spoken by a man; he has God himself as speaker.
17:
Teaching to profit is taken at its most ordinary. Ellicott hears the natural, perhaps the specially national, desire to make a good investment, and notes that men have answered the question what is profitable very differently, so the Redeemer's work is to lead them to the one imperishable gain. Wesley draws the conclusion the verse forces, that it is not God's fault but their own if they do not profit, since they knew their duty and cannot plead ignorance. Calvin sets the passage against an objection he expects: the people might complain that if God meant to help them he had better not have let them be carried off at all, since physicians who cure a disease they might have prevented are thought less entitled to thanks.

The wish that follows is handled carefully. Calvin hears an allusion to the song of Moses and takes the particle as a wish, then insists what kind: God expostulates, but also, like a father, deplores the wretchedness of his children, taking no pleasure in our distresses and being severe only when we constrain him. He calls it a figurative appropriation of human affections, then closes a door: it would be foolish to press into the secret counsel and ask why the efficacy of the Spirit was not added to the outward word, since nothing is said here about power and the verse is only a reproof. Keil and Delitzsch describe the stretch as hortatory, demanding fidelity and faith in the face of an approaching redemption.

Two of the comparisons get identified. Clarke and Ellicott both take the river to be the Euphrates, the natural standard for exiles living beside it, and Ellicott adds that righteousness here carries the blessedness that is its recompense. Both refuse the word gravel: the Hebrew says the bowels of the sea, which Clarke reports the Jewish expositors to mean fish, and Ellicott as creatures swarming in countless myriads. Wesley reads the waves as infinite and continual. Calvin refers the numbering back to the promise to Abraham and says the people prevented God from letting them enjoy its fruit. Ellicott hears in the two verses the sigh of every true teacher comparing what men are with what they might have been.

The summons out of Babylon is read at three distances. Ellicott keeps it historical: the sorrow is past, the prophet speaks to the returning remnant, who are to act at once on the promise and the decree and proclaim as they travel. Gill carries it forward to a mystical Babylon and the call by which men are brought out of confusion. Calvin attends to the manner rather than the object: we speak loudly of what we are certain of and are nearly dumb where we doubt, so the lofty language is itself designed to remove doubt from a promise that must have seemed incredible. Clarke adds only that many copies prefix a conjunction to the command.

Whether the water from the rock happened divides them three ways. Clarke reports a learned Jewish expositor wondering that no such miracles are recorded of the return, and marvels that a commentator so far into a work on this prophet could miss a parabolic style running from the first verse to the last; he asks why the historian was not expected to record cedars and olives springing up to shade the road. Ellicott calls the difficulty a dead prosaic literalism and takes the water as the standing symbol of spiritual refreshment. Calvin attacks the opposite fault, that the Jews invent miracles never performed, not through ignorance but presumption. On the closing line Calvin would repunctuate, so that God says to the wicked there is no peace, shutting hypocrites out of promises they would otherwise claim; Ellicott makes it an implied condition on every gift, since freedom and home are no blessing to the unworthy.
